fields.meta_title: Time Sheet Form That Totals Hours | Emergent
fields.meta_description: What a time sheet form should collect, how to set one up, and an app that deducts unpaid lunches and splits out overtime before approval.
fields.h1: Build a Time Sheet Form That Does the Math
fields.hero_description: A time sheet form records the hours someone worked each day, minus unpaid breaks. Emergent builds one around your pay period and the person who approves each sheet.
fields.features_heading: Hours Counted the Way Payroll Reads Them
fields.features_subheading: A printable sheet leaves the adding to whoever checks it on Friday. Emergent's version does the math as each day goes in.
fields.feature_1:
Daily totals from punch times

Turns each day's punch-in and punch-out times into hours, minus breaks, then adds the days into a week. Nobody types a total by hand, which is where most sheets go wrong.
fields.feature_2:
Unpaid meal breaks deducted

Subtracts meal breaks of 30 minutes or more and leaves short rest breaks in the day's hours. That is the line the Department of Labor draws between paid and unpaid breaks.
fields.feature_3:
Overtime kept in its own column

Moves any time beyond 40 hours in the workweek into a separate overtime column. The supervisor approves both figures together, and your payroll provider applies the rate.
fields.feature_4:
A job or client code on each entry

Asks for a job number or client code on every line and returns any entry left blank. Hours then roll up per code, ready for a job costing report or the next client invoice.
fields.feature_5:
Approval that locks the sheet

Sends each submitted sheet to the employee's supervisor in Slack or email. Approved entries lock, and any later edit needs a reason and records who changed it and when.
fields.feature_6:
Code you can take anywhere

Exports the full codebase to your GitHub repo. Your developers can add a payroll API sync or a kiosk clock-in screen, or ask Emergent for either one in a new prompt.

fields.usecase_heading: Time Sheet Forms by Type of Work
fields.tab_content_1:
Which of the 43.5 hours count as overtime

Warehouse weeks rarely end at 40. An associate works five days with a 30-minute unpaid lunch each day. The form deducts every lunch, totals the week at 43.5 hours and separates the 3.5 past 40. Federal law requires overtime pay for those hours, and the supervisor approves them as overtime first.
fields.tab_content_2:
Every hour lands on a job number

Construction payroll and job costing read the same sheet. A site foreman logs a crew of five against Job 2207 and Job 2214, and the form totals each job as entries arrive. One six-hour entry came in with no job code. It goes back to the worker to fix and stays out of both totals until then.
fields.tab_content_3:
Proof of each visit, signed by the client

Home care runs on visits, not shifts. An aide taps start when she arrives at a client's home and finish when she leaves. Before she goes, the client signs on her phone screen. The visit reaches the agency's scheduler with the signature attached, and its 2.5 hours land on the aide's time sheet.
fields.tab_content_4:
Who still owes a sheet by Monday

Payroll can only run on sheets that exist. The pay period closes Sunday night. On Monday morning a Slack message tells the office manager that 10 of 12 sheets are approved and two never came in. One click sends both people a reminder, and each late sheet goes to its supervisor once it is submitted.

fields.howto_title: How to Create a Time Sheet Form
fields.howto_description: Most time sheet errors come from typed totals and unclear break rules. These seven steps settle the rules first and leave the arithmetic to the form.
fields.howto_step_1_des: Choose the period payroll already runs on, usually weekly or biweekly. It sets how many rows the sheet needs and when it closes. Overtime is counted per workweek, and a biweekly sheet needs a subtotal for each of its two weeks.
fields.howto_step_2_des: Have people enter when they started and finished each day, plus the length of any break, instead of a typed total. Totals entered by hand drift by quarter hours. Times let the form do the math and show when each shift happened.
fields.howto_step_3_des: Under federal rules, a bona fide meal period of 30 minutes or more is usually unpaid, while short rest breaks count as hours worked. Give each its own field so the deduction is right and the employee can see it.
fields.howto_step_4_des: Keep regular hours and anything over 40 in a workweek in separate columns. Nonexempt employees earn at least time and a half for those extra hours under federal law. Check your state's rules too, then show both totals to the approver.
fields.howto_step_5_title: 05 Add job codes where hours get billed
fields.howto_step_5_des: When hours feed job costing or a client invoice, add a job or client code to each entry. Make it a dropdown of open jobs instead of free text. Entries with a blank code go back before the week closes.
fields.howto_step_6_title: 06 Route every sheet to one approver
fields.howto_step_6_des: Send each sheet to the employee's direct supervisor when the period ends, with a reminder for anyone who has not submitted by the next morning. Lock approved sheets so later edits need a reason and leave a trail.
fields.howto_step_7_des: Store every approved sheet and every edit in one place for at least two years, the retention period federal rules set for time cards. At each close, export approved hours to payroll split into regular and overtime.

plan.angle: The live SERP is printable templates (Pinterest, Template.net, Notion, a fillable PDF, Jotform's construction form) and an AI Overview listing the fields a time sheet needs. None of them adds the hours up for you or knows who still owes a sheet. This page answers what a time sheet form should collect and how to set one up, then builds what a template cannot: entries that total themselves with unpaid lunches deducted, hours past 40 flagged, hours tied to job numbers, client sign-off on a phone, and reminders before the pay period closes.
tab_stories: A warehouse associate clocks five days with a 30-minute unpaid lunch each day, the form totals the week at 43.5 hours and splits out the 3.5 hours past 40 for the supervisor to approve as overtime.
A site foreman logs a crew of five against two job numbers for the week, the board totals hours per job, and the one 6-hour entry with no job code goes back to the worker before the week closes.
A home care aide records a 2.5-hour visit on her phone, the client signs on the screen before she leaves, and the visit reaches the agency's scheduler with the signature attached.
The pay period closes Sunday night, 10 of 12 sheets are approved, and Monday morning the office manager sends reminders to the two people who have not submitted.

claims_to_source: Under the FLSA, covered nonexempt employees must receive overtime pay of at least one and one-half times the regular rate for hours worked over 40 in a workweek
Employers must keep records of hours worked each workday and total hours worked each workweek for nonexempt employees, and keep time cards for at least two years
Bona fide meal periods, typically 30 minutes or more, generally need not be compensated as work time, while short breaks of 5 to 20 minutes are counted as hours worked
A timecard is a record of an employee's starting and quitting times, typically stamped by a time clock
Microsoft offers free timesheet templates for Excel
Google Forms responses can be saved to a linked Google Sheets spreadsheet
Microsoft Teams Shifts includes a time clock that frontline workers use to clock in and out
